title: Writing a Fair Classroom AI Policy

thumbnail.headline: Red, Amber, Green AI
thumbnail.image: Navy background, a simple traffic light with red, amber and green circles beside a one-page policy sheet, headline in teal Inter Bold.

slide.title: Red, Amber, Green AI
slide.body: Icon of a traffic light next to a one-page document. Small tag: AI for Educators and Trainers · Lesson 4.

production_notes: [REGION] Institutional and local rules on AI use in education differ by country and institution. The voiceover tells learners to check their own rules and names no law.
The detection-tools point repeats L03 in cautious words ('can give false results'); it carries the same [VERIFY] as L03 and must be checked before recording.
Aiko Tanaka and her university in Osaka are fictional; stock footage must show no real university name or logo.
Use a consistent red, amber and green on every traffic-light slide, and also label each colour in words so the slides work for viewers with colour vision differences.

Hook.voiceover: One learner uses AI to check their grammar. Another uses it to write the whole essay. A third does not use it at all, because they are not sure it is allowed. If your learners cannot tell which is acceptable, your policy is not clear enough.

Explain.voiceover: In the last lesson, we looked at privacy and integrity. Now we turn that into rules learners can follow. A classroom AI policy tells learners when and how they may use AI in your course. Without one, learners guess, and different learners guess differently. That is unfair to everyone.

slide.title: Writing a Fair Classroom AI Policy
slide.body: AI for Educators and Trainers · Lesson 4 of 12. Three learner icons with question marks above their heads.

Explain.voiceover: A simple structure is the traffic-light model. For each type of task, you choose one of three colours. Red means AI is not allowed, because the task checks what the learner can do alone, like an in-class test.

slide.title: The traffic-light model
slide.body: Traffic light with the red circle lit. Label: Red = AI not allowed. Example: in-class written test, reflection on own experience.

Explain.voiceover: Amber means AI is allowed with disclosure. Learners may use it for certain steps, such as brainstorming or checking grammar, and they add a short note on what they asked and what they changed. Green means AI is allowed freely, for example to generate practice questions before a test.

slide.title: Amber and green
slide.body: Amber lit: AI allowed with disclosure (brainstorm, grammar check + short note). Green lit: AI allowed freely (practice questions to revise).

Explain.voiceover: A good policy is clear. Each rule names a task type, a colour and a short reason, in plain language, with examples of allowed and not allowed use.

slide.title: A good policy is clear
slide.body: Task type + colour + short reason · Plain language · Examples of allowed and not allowed use

Explain.voiceover: A good policy is also fair. It never requires paid tools, so every learner can complete green and amber tasks with a free tool or class time. Everyone knows the rules before the task begins. It explains disclosure, so honest learners are not punished for telling the truth. And it does not rely only on detection tools, which can give false results.

slide.title: A good policy is fair
slide.body: No paid tools required · Same rules, known in advance · Clear disclosure, no penalty for honesty · Not based only on detection tools

Explain.voiceover: And a good policy fits your institution. Your school, university or company may already have rules on AI, and local rules may apply too. Your course policy adds detail within those rules, and never contradicts them.
Explain.stock_query: staff meeting reviewing policy documents together

Explain.voiceover: Why traffic lights? Drivers do not read a long legal document at every crossing. Red, amber and green give a quick, shared signal. But the lights only work if they mean the same thing every time.
Explain.stock_query: traffic light at busy city crossing

Demonstrate.voiceover: Let's see an example. Aiko Tanaka teaches academic English to first-year students at a university in Osaka, in Japan. She drafts a policy for her writing course.
Demonstrate.stock_query: university students writing essays in lecture hall

Demonstrate.voiceover: The timed in-class essay is red, because it checks the student's own writing. The take-home essay is amber. AI may suggest ideas and correct grammar, with a note on how it was used. Vocabulary practice is green. And the reflection journal is red, because it must describe the student's own learning.

slide.title: Aiko's draft policy
slide.body: Table: Timed in-class essay | Red | own writing skills · Take-home essay | Amber | ideas and grammar + note · Vocabulary practice | Green | practice only · Reflection journal | Red | own experience

Demonstrate.voiceover: Then she pastes her draft, with no student information, into an AI assistant, and asks it to find rules that are unclear, or unfair to students with limited access to technology. It gives four suggestions.

slide.title: Aiko's check
slide.body: Find rules that are unclear or unfair to students with limited access to technology.  (Draft pasted below, no student information.)

Demonstrate.voiceover: Define what counts as AI. Does a spelling checker count? She accepts, and adds a short definition. Say what the disclosure note must include. She accepts, and adds a two-line template. Offer a free option or class time for green tasks. She accepts, and adds computer-room time.

slide.title: Suggestions she accepts
slide.body: Define 'AI' (does a spelling checker count?) → short definition added · What goes in the disclosure note → two-line template · Free option for green tasks → computer-room time

Demonstrate.voiceover: But the AI also suggests making the take-home essay red to prevent misuse. She rejects this. She wants students to learn responsible use, and she already includes a short conversation about each essay. Her final policy is still one page, and every decision is her own.

slide.title: A suggestion she rejects
slide.body: AI suggests: take-home essay → Red. Aiko: Rejected. Reason: students learn responsible use; a short conversation about each essay already checks the work.

Demonstrate.voiceover: A common mistake is one rule for the whole course, like AI is not allowed. It does not fit different tasks. Another is to accept every AI suggestion. You make the final judgement.
Demonstrate.on_screen_text: One rule does not fit every task

Recap.voiceover: Let's recap. First, a traffic-light policy gives each task type a colour, red, amber or green, with a short reason. Second, a fair policy does not require paid tools, explains disclosure clearly, and does not rely only on detection tools. Third, your policy must fit your institution's rules, and you decide which AI suggestions to accept.

slide.title: Key takeaways
slide.body: 1. Each task type: Red · Amber · Green + reason. 2. Fair: no paid tools, clear disclosure, not only detection. 3. Fits institutional rules; you decide.

CTA.voiceover: Now it is your turn. In the exercise below this video, draft a one-page traffic-light policy for a course you teach. Then ask Claude or ChatGPT to find unclear or unfair points, with no learner information, and decide which suggestions to accept. It takes about thirty minutes. In the next lesson, we start planning lessons with clear outcomes. See you there.
